title: DTCC Partners: Digital tools that support creative practice at Liljewall
abstract: For architecture firm Liljewall, its partnership with the Digital Twin Cities Centre, DTCC, provides an important bridge between research and practice. By translating research into tools that support the design process, Liljewall is strengthening its digital capabilities. One tangible outcome is an in-house simulation tool that helps architects assess cloudburst and stormwater risks at an early stage of a project.

body:
Liljewall has been involved in DTCC since the centre’s first phase and has contributed to several research projects. The collaboration has already generated practical results, including a tool for assessing cloudburst and stormwater risks. Liljewall is now participating in several new research initiatives, continuing its work to develop digital tools and methods that can be integrated into architectural practice.

“We have been part of DTCC from the beginning, so continuing as a partner in the centre’s second phase felt like a natural step. We continuously assess which areas of research are most relevant to us and how the findings can be applied in our own practice. I believe we have become skilled at identifying the elements that can deliver tangible value for our work,” says Cecilia Windh, Digitalisation Strategist and Urban Planner at Liljewall.

Liljewall takes a continuous and purpose-driven approach to digitalisation, focusing on tools and methods that support the creative process and contribute to better design outcomes.
“For us, digital tools are never the goal in themselves. They’re what we reach for when we need to understand, test or visualise something, and a digital approach is the best way to do it. DTCC’s breadth of research has been particularly valuable here,” says Ellen Simonsson, Architect at Liljewall.

**From research collaboration to an in-house tool**

One of the clearest outcomes of the partnership stems from Liljewall’s involvement in Urban Environmental Comfort Design, a project led by Franziska Hunger during DTCC’s first phase. Through the collaboration, Liljewall gained access to research on the simulation of cloudbursts and stormwater flows. The company subsequently used this knowledge as the basis for developing its own simulation tool.

The tool enables architects to explore how water is likely to move through an area during heavy rainfall. They can test alternative building locations, terrain modifications and measures for directing or collecting water, while receiving immediate visual feedback on how these decisions affect water flows.

“We wanted to create something that could be integrated into the early design process. If we move a building and see that a large volume of water is likely to accumulate in that location, we immediately know that the design needs to be reconsidered. We may need to raise the ground level, reposition the building or identify another way of managing the water,” says Ellen Simonsson.

Previously, this type of assessment would typically require the involvement of technical specialists and would often be conducted at a later stage in the project. The tool is not intended to replace a detailed stormwater analysis. Its value lies in providing architects with reliable information at an early stage, when there is still considerable scope to adjust the design.

“The tool is fast enough to use as part of the sketching process, while still providing results that are sufficiently reliable for that stage of a project. It can be introduced into an ongoing design process, and because it is visual and easy to use, it has also become a service that we can offer our clients,” says Cecilia Windh.

**Selecting research with a clear connection to practice**

During DTCC’s second phase, Liljewall is focusing on areas including climate adaptation, urban greenery, circular construction and new digital workflows. The company is participating in the Urban Trees and Reclaimed, Redesigned, Re-Twinned projects, while also following research in the mixed realities and digital construction areas.

“Greenery and trees are important areas for us and will be a particular focus during DTCC’s second phase. They contribute to the quality and comfort of urban environments, while also supporting heat management, improving wind conditions and promoting health. Much of our work is concerned with enriching places and understanding how people experience them, so engaging with this research is a natural next step for us,” says Cecilia Windh.

**Moving reuse from inventory to design**

Circular construction is another important area for Liljewall. During DTCC’s first phase, the company participated in Twin Re-Fab, a project led by Malgorzata Zboinska that explored digital methods for scanning existing buildings and materials. In the new phase, Liljewall aims to follow this work further through its involvement in Reclaimed, Redesigned, Re-Twinned.
The project explores how broken bricks, glass fragments, tiles and complete building components can be treated as resources for new construction rather than as waste. For Liljewall, the research addresses practical questions that are becoming increasingly significant in real-world projects. These include how materials should be inventoried, scanned, tagged and stored, how they can be located when needed, and how their environmental and economic benefits can be evaluated.

“What I hope we will gain is a better understanding of the entire process. If we can develop a process and a method that we understand and are able to use independently, the impact will extend far beyond a single successful project. It can become an integral part of how we approach design,” says Ellen Simonsson.

**Building the architectural practice of the future**

Liljewall’s involvement in DTCC has generated value in several ways. In addition to participating in applied research, the company has gained access to professional networks and to the collective expertise represented within the centre.

“What I particularly appreciate about DTCC is its willingness to listen to the needs of practitioners and to understand the conditions in which we work. There is an openness that allows us to explore the same overall research themes while adapting the work to our own professional context. This gives the collaboration clear practical value,” says Cecilia Windh.

This practical relevance is one of the reasons Liljewall has chosen to continue its involvement in DTCC, despite the considerable economic pressure currently facing the architecture industry. Research and development require both time and resources, but Liljewall views the investment as an important part of maintaining its relevance and competitiveness over the long term.

“We have seen sufficient benefits to know that continuing the collaboration is worthwhile. We are choosing to prioritise internal research and development because, even while addressing today’s challenges, we also need to consider where we want to be in five or ten years. We have become increasingly effective at translating research findings into practical applications, and DTCC has played an important role in that development,” says Cecilia Windh.
